questions.question: Why must large molecules like proteins and fats be broken down during digestion?
options: Because cells can only use them if they are split into smaller molecules first.
To allow them to be absorbed through the gut wall into the body.
To prevent them from being attacked by helpful bacteria in the stomach.
To make sure they can dissolve in the water inside the mouth.

questions.question: Once nutrients are absorbed into the blood, what is their primary destination and purpose?
options: They are stored permanently in the blood vessels to keep the blood thick.
They are transported around the body to cells that need them.
They are carried directly to the kidneys to be filtered out of the body immediately.
They are taken to the lungs to be mixed with oxygen before entering any cells.

questions.question: Some nutrients can move from the small intestine into the blood by diffusion. Which statement best describes how this happens?
options: Particles move from an area of lower concentration in the intestine to a higher concentration in the blood, requiring energy.
Particles are actively pumped through specialized valves in the intestine wall.
Particles move from an area of higher concentration in the intestine to a lower concentration in the blood.
Particles are carried by water currents through large pores without any concentration difference.

questions.question: Which of the following describes how the lining of the small intestine is adapted to maximize the absorption of nutrients?
options: It is perfectly smooth and thick to prevent nutrients from escaping too quickly.
It has a very large surface area due to finger-like projections called villi.
It is covered in a thick layer of acid-resistant mucus that slows down digestion.
It is extremely short, allowing food to pass through as quickly as possible.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most accurate description of a bacterium?
options: A non-living particle made of proteins and genetic material.
A multicellular organism that lacks a true cellular structure.
A microorganism made of a single living cell.
A specialized human cell designed to fight off infections.

questions.question: Which statement best represents the diversity of bacteria in relation to human health?
options: All bacteria are pathogens that cause harmful infectious diseases.
Some bacteria cause disease, but many are harmless and some are actually helpful.
Bacteria are only helpful to humans and never cause any kind of illness.
Bacteria only become harmful when they are inside the stomach acid.

questions.question: Where in the human body would you find a large population of helpful bacteria that assist with digestion?
options: Inside the salivary glands in the mouth.
Inside the human digestive system.
Inside the windpipe and lungs.
On the dry outer surface of the teeth.

questions.question: How do the helpful bacteria living in our digestive system assist in digesting foods that we cannot digest ourselves?
options: They physically grind the food into smaller pieces using cellular teeth.
They release enzymes that break down these complex food molecules.
They absorb the food whole and carry it directly into our bloodstream.
They produce acid that dissolves the food instantly.

questions.question: In what way do helpful gut bacteria protect us against harmful pathogens that enter our digestive system?
options: They produce antibodies that destroy all foreign cells.
They build physical walls around the pathogens to trap them.
They compete against the pathogens for resources and space.
They signal the brain to raise the body's temperature immediately.

questions.question: Compare mechanical and chemical digestion. Which of the following correctly describes a difference between them?
options: Mechanical digestion only occurs in the stomach, while chemical digestion only occurs in the mouth.
Mechanical digestion physically breaks food into smaller pieces, whereas chemical digestion uses enzymes to break chemical bonds.
Mechanical digestion turns food into completely new substances, while chemical digestion only changes its shape.
Chemical digestion is carried out by muscles, while mechanical digestion is carried out by hormones.

questions.question: What are the three main groups of molecules that make up the food we eat?
options: Minerals, vitamins, and water.
Carbohydrates, proteins, and fats.
Sugars, starches, and fiber.
Enzymes, acids, and saliva.

questions.question: What is the primary role of enzymes during the chemical digestion of carbohydrates, proteins, and fats?
options: They act as fuel to provide energy for the digestive organs.
They act as biological catalysts to speed up the breakdown of these molecules.
They physically squeeze the food to break it into smaller parts.
They lower the temperature of the stomach to prevent burning.

questions.question: According to the digestive processes of the body, what are proteins and fats broken down into, respectively?
options: Sugars and starch.
Fatty acids/glycerol and amino acids.
Amino acids and fatty acids/glycerol.
Carbohydrates and proteins.

questions.question: A student wants to test a food sample to see if it contains starch (a large carbohydrate molecule). Which chemical reagent should they use?
options: Benedict's solution.
Iodine solution.
Biuret reagent.
Ethanol.

questions.question: To test for the presence of simple sugars (small molecules) resulting from the breakdown of starch, which reagent and condition should be used?
options: Iodine solution at room temperature.
Benedict's solution with heating.
Biuret reagent with shaking.
Ethanol mixed with cold water.

questions.question: During a food test experiment, a student adds Biuret reagent to a liquid food sample and observes a color change from blue to lilac/purple. What does this result indicate?
options: The food sample contains a high amount of starch.
The food sample contains protein.
The food sample contains simple sugars.
The food sample contains lipids/fats.

questions.question: Which of the following represents the correct sequence of major organs that food passes through after it is swallowed?
options: Oesophagus -> Stomach -> Small Intestine -> Large Intestine.
Stomach -> Oesophagus -> Large Intestine -> Small Intestine.
Oesophagus -> Small Intestine -> Stomach -> Large Intestine.
Stomach -> Small Intestine -> Oesophagus -> Large Intestine.

questions.question: How is the stomach specifically adapted to carry out its function in the digestive system?
options: It has thin, transparent walls to let light in for chemical reactions.
It has a muscular wall to churn food and produces acid and enzymes to break down food.
It is lined with villi to absorb the majority of digested nutrients into the blood.
It produces bile to neutralize acid before the food enters the mouth.

questions.question: What happens to the parts of the food we eat that cannot be digested by our enzymes or bacteria?
options: They are absorbed into the blood and filtered out by the lungs.
They are converted into liquid urine in the kidneys.
They are passed out of the body as faeces.
They remain in the stomach permanently to help digest future food.

questions.question: A student adds iodine solution to a piece of bread and it turns blue-black. They also heat a sample of milk with Benedict's solution and it remains blue. What can be concluded about the bread and milk?
options: The bread contains starch, and the milk does not contain detectable reducing sugars.
The bread contains protein, and the milk contains starch.
The bread has no starch, and the milk has a high sugar content.
Both the bread and the milk contain large amounts of fat.
